name: Swap the subject with another noun
what_it_does: Replaces the repeated subject with a different noun already in the sentence so the sentence opens on something new.
bad_example: I met Jack at the mall.
good_example: Jack met me at the mall.
why_it_works: The same event is reported, but the opening word changes and the emphasis shifts to a different participant.
when_to_use: When several consecutive sentences start with the same subject and the meaning allows another noun to perform the action.
for_written_prose: yes, because it is a pure syntax swap that works identically on the page.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Make the action the subject
what_it_does: Turns the action itself into the grammatical subject so the sentence opens on the deed rather than the doer.
bad_example: I threw a punch at Jack but missed.
good_example: My punch sailed wide of Jack's face.
why_it_works: It removes the repeated 'I' and gives the reader a concrete visual of the action.
when_to_use: In fast-paced fight or action scenes with many short sentences.
for_written_prose: yes, because action scenes are written prose and the visual lands the same way.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Make the sensory detail the subject
what_it_does: Promotes the thing seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or felt to the subject position so the sentence opens on the sensation.
bad_example: I saw a vibrant painting.
good_example: A vibrant painting caught my eye.
why_it_works: Sensory details draw readers into the story, and making them the subject removes the repeated perceiver.
when_to_use: Whenever you are describing sights, sounds, smells, tastes, or physical feelings.
for_written_prose: yes, because sensory description is a core prose tool.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Front the adjective
what_it_does: Moves an adjective that describes the subject to the very start of the sentence.
bad_example: I went to bed hungry.
good_example: Hungry, I went to bed.
why_it_works: The adjective still describes the subject, but the opening word changes and the state is emphasized first.
when_to_use: In a pinch, when you need a quick variation and the adjective is short and clear.
when_it_backfires: The video notes it is not the most exciting or smoothest option.
for_written_prose: yes, because it is a standard inverted sentence pattern.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Front the adverb
what_it_does: Moves an adverb describing how or when the action happens to the start of the sentence.
bad_example: I hopelessly tried unlocking the safe.
good_example: Hopelessly, I tried unlocking the safe.
why_it_works: The adverb still modifies the verb, but the sentence now opens on the manner or time of the action.
when_to_use: When an adverb of manner or time can lead the sentence without sounding awkward.
for_written_prose: yes, because adverb-fronting is ordinary written syntax.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Front the participial phrase
what_it_does: Opens the sentence with an -ing verb phrase that describes the subject.
bad_example: I tried to get the waitress's attention by shouting.
good_example: Shouting, I tried to get the waitress's attention.
why_it_works: It varies the opening and adds an image the reader can grab onto.
when_to_use: When you want to spice up the opening and add a simultaneous action or image.
for_written_prose: yes, because participial openers are common in written prose.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Front a time-based prepositional phrase
what_it_does: Moves a prepositional phrase about when something happens to the beginning of the sentence.
bad_example: I hunt vampires in the evening.
good_example: In the evening, I hunt vampires.
why_it_works: Time phrases move smoothly to the front and change the opening without distorting the sentence.
when_to_use: When the prepositional phrase is based on time, such as 'in the evening' or 'after the game'.
when_it_backfires: Do not move location-based prepositional phrases; 'Over the hurdle, I jumped' sounds like Yoda.
for_written_prose: yes, because time-fronting is standard in written prose.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Front the dependent clause
what_it_does: Moves a clause that needs another sentence to the front so the sentence opens on the subordinate idea.
bad_example: I stopped running when she called out to me.
good_example: When she called out to me, I stopped running.
why_it_works: The clause relocates easily and both versions remain effective and clear.
when_to_use: When the dependent clause can stand at the front without confusing the sequence of events.
for_written_prose: yes, because dependent-clause fronting is ordinary written syntax.
source_title: 8 Tips for Starting Better Sentences (Writing Advice)

name: Find the less obvious but smarter answer
what_it_does: Replaces the expected, literal response to a brief with a sharper idea the requester missed.
bad_example: Answer exactly what you've been asked, following the brief literally like every competitor.
good_example: Ask: is there a less obvious but smarter answer? Do I see something my boss missed?
why_it_works: If everyone follows the same brief, the audience sits through ten versions of the same idea, so a different angle stands out.
when_to_use: Before building any pitch, proposal, or response to senior leadership.
for_written_prose: partly — the reframing works in writing, but you lose the live read of the room.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Speak with authority
what_it_does: Signals conviction through slow, measured speech, neutral sentence endings, and controlled gestures.
bad_example: Lifting your voice at the end of sentences as if asking for approval or permission.
good_example: Slow, measured voice, neutral tone at sentence ends, hands kept in the zone of authority.
why_it_works: Delivery that says 'I know where I'm going, just follow me' removes the scent of doubt that invites resistance.
when_to_use: Whenever you present an idea you need others to trust.
for_written_prose: no — this is a vocal and physical move that has no direct page equivalent.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Bring in a respected third party
what_it_does: Challenges someone's thinking without making it you versus them.
bad_example: I think we're looking at this the wrong way.
good_example: I recently came across a Stanford study showing storytelling is about seven times more memorable than facts alone.
why_it_works: It reframes the challenge as a lesson from an expert, customer, mentor, or data point rather than a personal attack.
when_to_use: When you need to push back on a client's or boss's stated direction.
for_written_prose: yes — citing a study or mentor works equally well on the page.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Deliver the lesson through story
what_it_does: Wraps the idea in a person and a moment so the audience gets curious instead of defensive.
bad_example: Here is the concept I recommend we use for this campaign.
good_example: My first job, I was in-house at a fur company with this old pro copywriter, Greek, named Teddy.
why_it_works: A person and a story create curiosity about what the wise figure taught, which buys time instead of triggering argument.
when_to_use: When introducing an idea that contradicts what the audience expects.
for_written_prose: yes — narrative framing carries directly to the page.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Make them feel it, not just see it
what_it_does: Turns an abstract idea into felt emotion using sensory, human language instead of jargon.
bad_example: Nostalgia is a stronger positioning than new technology for this product.
good_example: The pain from an old wound. A twinge in your heart, far more powerful than memory alone.
why_it_works: Stronger emotional response in an audience leads to more action afterward than logical argument alone.
when_to_use: When you need genuine buy-in and motivation to act, not just agreement.
for_written_prose: yes — sensory language and personal detail translate directly to prose.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Show your own vulnerability
what_it_does: Removes you from the role of adversary by making the emotion personal.
bad_example: You should consider how customers feel about this product.
good_example: Showing photographs from his own life — his wife, his children, moments that have already passed.
why_it_works: Personal exposure makes the speaker a participant in the feeling rather than an opponent arguing a case.
when_to_use: When the idea you're selling is emotional and you risk seeming like you're just debating.
for_written_prose: partly — first-person detail works on the page, but the live vulnerability of the moment is diminished.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Land it with a sound bite
what_it_does: Compresses the whole idea into a short, sharp, catchy, memorable sentence.
bad_example: This projector is a new kind of technology that lets people revisit the past.
good_example: This device isn't a spaceship. It's a time machine.
why_it_works: A short, rhythmic contrast sticks in memory and gives the audience a phrase to carry the idea with.
when_to_use: At the moment you want the idea to land and be remembered.
for_written_prose: yes — sound bites are equally effective in written prose.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Build a bridge before the new name
what_it_does: Expands the object into something bigger before revealing the reframed label.
bad_example: Let's call it the carousel instead of the wheel.
good_example: It lets us travel the way a child travels, around and around and back home again.
why_it_works: The audience feels the meaning first, so the new name seems discovered rather than invented.
when_to_use: When renaming or reframing something the audience already has a fixed label for.
for_written_prose: yes — the bridge-then-name sequence works in writing.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Let the silence linger
what_it_does: Stops talking after the idea lands so the audience can process it.
bad_example: Explaining the idea one more time or probing to see how the pitch was perceived.
good_example: He has done his work, said what he needed to, and lets the silence linger.
why_it_works: Silence used well demonstrates authority and self-confidence and lets the new concept settle.
when_to_use: Immediately after your idea has landed.
for_written_prose: no — silence is a live-room move; on the page you'd need white space or a hard stop instead.
source_title: How to Sell Your Ideas Better Than 99% of Your Colleagues

name: Use evidence to support claims
what_it_does: Backs up a character's opinions or assumptions with the concrete evidence that led them there.
bad_example: Adam knew Gwen liked him.
good_example: Between classes Gwen was always leaned on his locker; the combination lock still warm from her ass.
why_it_works: Readers deduce the conclusion themselves, which makes them feel and think what the character does.
when_to_use: Whenever a character forms an assumption, opinion, or belief about someone or something.
for_written_prose: yes, this is a prose technique about replacing thought verbs with dramatized evidence.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Replace the abstract with the concrete
what_it_does: Swaps stated emotions and opinion adjectives for actions and details that let the reader infer the feeling.
bad_example: After his first kiss, Toby walked home feeling happier than he'd ever felt in all his thirteen years.
good_example: Toby couldn't keep the goofy grin off his face; at the front gate he jumped clean over it.
why_it_works: Abstract concepts like happiness must be demonstrated with concrete details the reader can visualize.
when_to_use: When you catch yourself directly stating a character's feelings or using opinion adjectives like beautiful or strange.
for_written_prose: yes, it is a sentence-level revision move for prose.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Substitute vague descriptions with specific sensory details
what_it_does: Replaces generic visual descriptions with unique, multi-sensory details that make scenes immersive.
bad_example: Aga walked through the market, gaping at the rugs and bins of spices.
good_example: Spicy cinnamon and rich coffee rode the air as she ran her fingers down silken tassels and through powdery barrels of golden saffron.
why_it_works: Specific sensory details make feelings and scenes jump off the page and feel unique to the story.
when_to_use: When a description creates a mental image but doesn't invoke senses beyond sight or feels generic.
for_written_prose: yes, sensory specificity is a core prose technique.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Avoid relying too much on body language
what_it_does: Shows emotion through a character's thought process and interactions with the setting rather than visceral physical reactions.
bad_example: Her heart nearly leapt out of her chest. Her stomach rolled over when she remembered.
good_example: She wouldn't think about Billy. The doctor said it wouldn't happen again. The odds against it were astronomical.
why_it_works: Thoughts lead to emotions and emotions lead to actions; readers deduce emotions from what characters think and do.
when_to_use: In highly emotional scenes where you want emotional nuance rather than shorthand.
when_it_backfires: Common facial expressions and gestures are great for quickly conveying mood but rarely evoke an emotional response from the reader.
for_written_prose: yes, it is about prose pacing and interiority.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Show emotion through dialogue
what_it_does: Lets a character's words and tone convey their feelings instead of narrating the emotion or using adverbs.
bad_example: Mary was angry at Bob. "You wretched picklemonger," she shouted angrily.
good_example: "You wretched picklemonger. How dare you!" she shouted.
why_it_works: The words alone show the tone and volume, so adverbs and intent tags tell the reader what they've already shown.
when_to_use: When writing emotional dialogue; try drafting it as a play or screenplay to force emotion through dialogue alone.
for_written_prose: yes, dialogue is a prose tool, though the play-drafting trick is a writing exercise.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Filter observations through the narrative voice
what_it_does: Lets a character's emotions color how they see their surroundings, making exposition feel in-world rather than dictionary-like.
bad_example: The rain poured down the window. Bob sat at the table, a stack of pancakes beside him.
good_example: The rain beat against the restaurant window like rounds from an Uzi. Bob sat with his back against the wall.
why_it_works: Giving details through the point-of-view character's perspective connects the reader more closely to what they're experiencing.
when_to_use: When presenting world-building, backstory, or infodumps that might otherwise read as authorial explanation.
for_written_prose: yes, it is about point of view and exposition in prose.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Use the camera test
what_it_does: Checks whether a detail can be visualized by asking if a camera could see it.
bad_example: The dark forest felt eerie.
good_example: The forest hummed with the cries of children long dead.
why_it_works: Almost all showing contains a detail that can be visualized, often combined with smell, touch, taste, and sound.
when_to_use: When identifying whether you're in abstract territory during revision.
for_written_prose: yes, it is a revision check for prose.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Show the effect, not the cause
what_it_does: Describes how a condition affects a character rather than stating the condition itself.
bad_example: The temperature fell and the ice reflected the sun.
good_example: Bill's nose burned in the frigid air, and he squinted against the sun reflecting off the street.
why_it_works: Details shown through how the character interacts with the world make the scene more visual.
when_to_use: When describing weather, setting, or physical states that could be shown through a character's reaction.
for_written_prose: yes, it is a descriptive prose technique.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Replace 'was' and 'felt' with stronger verbs
what_it_does: Flags spots where a stronger verb could create a concrete image instead of an adjective following 'was' or 'felt'.
bad_example: She was uncomfortable around him. The house was huge. She was hungry.
good_example: She stiffened in his embrace. His whole family could live in the kitchen alone. She near-inhaled the soup.
why_it_works: 'Was' and 'felt' are often followed by adjectives, signaling a spot where a stronger verb can create a concrete image.
when_to_use: During revision when you spot 'was' or 'felt' followed by an adjective.
for_written_prose: yes, it is a sentence-level prose revision technique.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Avoid 'As You Know, Bob' exposition
what_it_does: Prevents characters from explaining things to each other that they already know, which pulls the reader out of the story.
bad_example: No, you know how today we're heading into the land of the Giants to offer them the Jewel of Valencia?
good_example: Kevin, where'd you learn to make bombs?" "The Navy.
why_it_works: Characters have prior knowledge outside the narrative; including less detail in dialogue feels more realistic.
when_to_use: When dialogue feels like information given for the reader's sake rather than something the character would realistically say.
for_written_prose: yes, dialogue is a prose element.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Slow down emotional scenes
what_it_does: Lets the reader hear every thought, highlights a few details, and shows actions during highly emotional moments.
bad_example: Not stated.
good_example: Not stated.
why_it_works: When you have a very emotional scene, slowing it down lets readers experience the character's full thought process.
when_to_use: During very emotional scenes where you want readers to feel the moment deeply.
for_written_prose: yes, it is about prose pacing.
source_title: How to Show, Not Tell: The Complete Writing Guide

name: Feel the discomfort
what_it_does: Allows you to notice the physical sensation of fear or anxiety without letting it drive your behavior.
bad_example: I feel nervous, so I'll just say yes and avoid the conflict.
good_example: I notice I'm uncomfortable, but I'm not going to act based on this feeling. I'll speak up anyway.
why_it_works: Observing the discomfort creates a gap between feeling and action, so fear no longer dictates your response.
when_to_use: When you notice yourself wanting to avoid a necessary conversation or say yes when you mean no.
for_written_prose: partly
source_title: How to Speak Up at Work So People Respect You

name: Intervene early
what_it_does: Speak up at the first sign of an issue rather than waiting until resentment builds and you explode.
bad_example: I'll wait and hope the problem resolves itself, then react when I'm angry.
good_example: I'll address this now, before it becomes a bigger problem, even though it's uncomfortable.
why_it_works: Early intervention prevents the accumulation of resentment that leads to emotional outbursts and damaged relationships.
when_to_use: When you first notice a boundary being crossed or a performance issue arising.
for_written_prose: partly
source_title: How to Speak Up at Work So People Respect You

name: Reduce words
what_it_does: Say what you need to say simply and clearly, without over-explaining, over-apologizing, or rambling.
bad_example: I was thinking it might be a good idea if we were to follow this strategy because...
good_example: This strategy should work because the data says so.
why_it_works: Simplicity and clarity convey conviction and respect, while excessive words signal anxiety and undermine your message.
when_to_use: When giving feedback, setting a boundary, or making a request, especially if you feel anxious.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: How to Speak Up at Work So People Respect You

name: Maintain boundaries
what_it_does: State what you are willing to tolerate and consistently uphold that limit when tested.
bad_example: You're overreacting. I'm not too sensitive. I'll just stay and take it.
good_example: Like I said, I'm not okay with this. I will come back in 5 minutes when we've had a chance to calm down.
why_it_works: Consistently maintaining boundaries builds respect and authority, while engaging with pushback undermines your position.
when_to_use: When someone crosses a line you've set, such as shouting or disrespect.
for_written_prose: partly
source_title: How to Speak Up at Work So People Respect You

name: Lead with the main point
what_it_does: Cuts through rambling by stating the core idea first, before context or background.
bad_example: Before I get to my recommendation, I just want to give a little bit of background because there's a lot of nuance here...
good_example: I recommend that we delay the launch by 2 weeks. Here's why.
why_it_works: Clarity is associated with competence; concise, simple language makes speakers seem more capable even if they are not.
when_to_use: Any time you have a recommendation, update, or key idea to deliver in a meeting or conversation.
for_written_prose: yes — leading with the point works in emails, reports, and essays, though the exact phrasing may need adjustment.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Stop after the point
what_it_does: Prevents overexplaining by ending your statement once the main idea is made, without caveats or justifications.
bad_example: I recommend that we simplify the onboarding process. I mean, I could be missing something, and I know I don't know what you guys think...
good_example: I think the onboarding process is too complex. We are losing people in the first 5 minutes. I recommend that we simplify.
why_it_works: Over-justifying communicates uncertainty; confident communicators let the idea sit and give listeners processing time.
when_to_use: After making a recommendation or stating an opinion, especially when you feel tempted to soften or defend it.
for_written_prose: yes — in writing, ending after the point avoids weakening your message with unnecessary caveats.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Let silence sit
what_it_does: Uses intentional pauses after making a point to project composure and give others time to reflect.
bad_example: I think we should move forward with option B because... well, it's the best fit and I don't know. I mean, what do you guys think?
good_example: I recommend that we move forward with option B. [pause]
why_it_works: Controlled, intentional pauses are perceived as confidence and calm, signaling that you are comfortable waiting.
when_to_use: Immediately after finishing a key point, especially in meetings or presentations.
for_written_prose: partly — silence translates to white space or short paragraphs in writing, but the effect is weaker than in speech.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Cut softening phrases
what_it_does: Removes words and phrases that dilute your message and signal low conviction.
bad_example: Just a thought, I could be wrong, but maybe this is obvious... does that make sense?
good_example: I recommend that we simplify the onboarding process.
why_it_works: Softening language teaches people to take your ideas less seriously because it signals you lack conviction.
when_to_use: In any communication where you want to be taken seriously, including meetings, emails, and casual conversations.
for_written_prose: yes — especially relevant in written communication, where words like 'just' often creep in.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Reclaim the floor
what_it_does: Calmly addresses interruptions by asserting your right to finish your point before yielding.
bad_example: [Going silent and not finishing your point when interrupted]
good_example: Just let me finish my point and I'll come to you.
why_it_works: Allowing interruptions trains people to treat you as someone who can be cut off; calmly reclaiming the floor shifts the dynamic.
when_to_use: When someone interrupts you repeatedly or in a pattern, not for every single interruption.
when_it_backfires: Not stated, but the video notes not to interpret this as being combative or policing every conversation.
for_written_prose: no — this is a live speaking move for managing real-time interruptions.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Use downward inflection
what_it_does: Ends statements with a falling tone instead of a rising one, making them sound like facts rather than questions.
bad_example: I recommend that we delay our launch by two weeks? [upward inflection]
good_example: I recommend that we delay our launch by two weeks. [downward inflection]
why_it_works: Upward inflection makes statements sound like questions, signaling uncertainty; downward inflection conveys conviction.
when_to_use: When making statements, recommendations, or declarations in any spoken communication.
for_written_prose: no — this is purely a vocal technique with no direct written equivalent.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Speak with your hands in the authority zone
what_it_does: Uses hand gestures within the space between shoulders and hips to appear more compelling and confident.
bad_example: [Hands rigidly by your sides, arms crossed, or shrinking yourself]
good_example: [Using hand gestures in the zone between your shoulder and hips while speaking]
why_it_works: People are more compelling when they use hand gestures in the authority zone; this also makes you feel more confident.
when_to_use: During presentations, meetings, or any spoken communication where you want to project authority.
for_written_prose: no — body language does not translate to written prose.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: Slow down and be still
what_it_does: Reduces fast movements, fidgeting, and rapid speech to project calm and composure.
bad_example: [Speaking quickly, using many fast hand gestures, fidgeting with nervous movements]
good_example: [Speaking at a measured pace, using deliberate gestures, staying still]
why_it_works: Fast movements and speech signal anxiety and lack of calm, which undermines perceived authority.
when_to_use: Whenever you notice yourself feeling anxious or speaking quickly, especially in high-stakes situations.
for_written_prose: no — this is a physical and vocal technique for live delivery.
source_title: How to Speak with Authority So People Instantly Respect You

name: State your point clearly and concisely
what_it_does: Delivers your situation and recommendation in the first 15–30 seconds using four sentences or fewer, then pauses.
bad_example: So, I'm thinking we should probably simplify our onboarding process. Could be wrong, happy to hear your opinion.
good_example: Our data clearly shows that our onboarding process is too complex. I strongly recommend we simplify it.
why_it_works: It establishes authority before the audience has assessed your argument, avoiding the need to ask permission to hold your opinion.
when_to_use: At the start of any important recommendation or presentation.
when_it_backfires: When it turns confidence into bluffing; being clear about uncertainty is different from sounding uncertain in every sentence.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Finish your sentences like statements
what_it_does: Eliminates rising intonation (up talk) at the end of statements so they sound like declarations, not questions.
bad_example: I recommend we delay the launch by two weeks? (with rising pitch)
good_example: I recommend we delay the launch by two weeks. (with falling pitch)
why_it_works: Listeners link rising intonation to lower perceived confidence and authority; a statement gives the room something to act on.
when_to_use: Whenever you make a recommendation or state a fact in a meeting.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; occasional use is fine, but a repetitive pattern should be changed.
for_written_prose: no
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Replace hesitations with silence
what_it_does: Removes filler words (um, uh, like, you know) and replaces them with well-placed pauses, especially after key points.
bad_example: So um I want to uh propose um a new way of advancing our uh program.
good_example: I want to propose a new way of advancing our program. [pause]
why_it_works: Silence commands more authority than any filler word, and people who speak with credibility speak less, slower, and with minimal hesitations.
when_to_use: In any spoken communication, particularly after a key point or unexpected information.
for_written_prose: no
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Don't oversell; use clear checkpoints
what_it_does: Avoids vague promises and instead specifies concrete, time-bound deliverables so the room can watch you land what you said.
bad_example: You could promise a three-story beautiful house by March, but then hand over two stories in December.
good_example: On Thursday, I'll have a SWOT analysis ready. Within a week, you'll get the amended business plan. Project complete in 8–10 weeks maximum.
why_it_works: Each checkpoint gives the room a chance to see you deliver, which builds trust and credibility faster than vague vision-selling.
when_to_use: When making commitments, pitching a vision, or leading a team.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video warns that overselling damages reputation and leads to gossip.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Be mindful of your body language
what_it_does: Adopts prestige signals—slight chest expansion, head tilted up, a little smile—rather than dominance signals like downward head tilt, no smile, and spread limbs.
bad_example: Sinking down, leaning backwards, making yourself smaller in the room.
good_example: Sitting up straight with shoulders back, head straight, smiling, engaging.
why_it_works: Strangers recognize these displays within seconds, and they communicate authority and credibility before you speak.
when_to_use: In any important meeting or room where you need to be taken seriously.
for_written_prose: no
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Name the elephant in the room
what_it_does: Discloses bad news or a crisis directly before anyone else can reveal it, then immediately offers a proposed solution.
bad_example: Waiting for others to reveal the crisis, or delivering bad news with filler words, hesitation, and excuses.
good_example: Go straight to the point, no filler words, no hesitation, no excuses, posture held, and a proposed solution right behind the bad news.
why_it_works: Honesty is central to credibility; organizations that disclosed their own crisis first scored significantly higher on credibility.
when_to_use: When you have bad news to deliver or a crisis to address.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; an excuse is acceptable only if truly warranted.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Focus on the decision, not on yourself
what_it_does: Puts your ego away and operates in service of the business and the decision that needs to be taken, rather than trying to look good.
bad_example: Asking yourself in the corridor how you're going to come across, or changing your recommendation to protect your image.
good_example: Before the meeting, answer: What does this person need from me today and what decision are we here to make?
why_it_works: Experienced people can tell the difference between someone using signals to serve the decision and someone using them to be seen; trust is inferred from visible behaviors.
when_to_use: Before and during any meeting where you want to build credibility.
when_it_backfires: The first five rules can backfire if your intention is wrong; no amount of technique will buy you the room if you consistently act against trust.
for_written_prose: partly
source_title: How to Speak with Credibility So People Respect You

name: Open with a surprising statistic
what_it_does: Signals urgency, tension, or opportunity with a single compelling piece of data before any self-introduction.
bad_example: Hi everyone, I'm Shannon Jenkins from digital strategy. Today I'll be talking about how we can optimize website efficiency.
good_example: 40 million francs. That is how much we spend on websites every single year. It is far worse than the industry average.
why_it_works: The number makes the audience immediately understand the scale of the problem and what is at stake.
when_to_use: When you have one convincing piece of data that frames the whole talk.
for_written_prose: yes — a striking statistic can open an essay or report just as effectively.
source_title: How to Start a Presentation So NOBODY Checks Their Phone!

name: Open with audience interaction
what_it_does: Asks the audience a question at the very start to move them from passive to active mode.
bad_example: Hi everyone, I'm Shannon Jenkins, head of digital transformation, and today I'll present our website plan.
good_example: How much do you think we spend on websites annually? 10 million, 20 million, or 40 million? Hands up if you think it's 20 million.
why_it_works: Making people respond physically or in chat reduces multitasking and phone-checking by forcing participation.
when_to_use: In person with a show of hands, virtually via chat, or in small meetings by asking people directly.
for_written_prose: partly — a direct question to the reader can work, but live polling and show of hands do not carry to the page.
source_title: How to Start a Presentation So NOBODY Checks Their Phone!

name: Lead with the audience outcome
what_it_does: Opens by naming the benefit the audience will gain from listening, rather than the topic you will cover.
bad_example: Hi everyone, I'm Shannon Jenkins. Thank you for being here. Today I'm going to talk to you about storytelling.
good_example: There is one communication tool that will make people engage with you, increase your influence, and make your message seven times more likely to be remembered. That tool is storytelling.
why_it_works: People pay attention when they can see exactly what they have to gain from listening.
when_to_use: As a default introduction, especially when the topic alone is not obviously compelling to the audience.
for_written_prose: yes — leading with the reader's benefit works in articles, emails, and reports.
source_title: How to Start a Presentation So NOBODY Checks Their Phone!

name: Open with a story
what_it_does: Drops the audience into a specific human moment instead of abstract corporate language.
bad_example: Good morning everyone. Today I'm going to walk you through the updated mental health and well-being frameworks, including revised psychological safety protocols.
good_example: Two weeks ago I walked into the office and saw an email from a colleague sent at 2:37 a.m. Later he had a distant blank look. Yesterday he was signed off with burnout.
why_it_works: Stories shift people from analyzing business as usual to experiencing, making the message concrete, emotional, and memorable.
when_to_use: When you have a short, real moment that connects directly to your main message.
for_written_prose: yes — a concrete anecdote opens prose just as powerfully as a talk.
source_title: How to Start a Presentation So NOBODY Checks Their Phone!

name: Open with a prop, visual, or activity
what_it_does: Starts with something visual, interactive, or unexpected that creates curiosity and links to the main message.
bad_example: I'm just going to wait a couple of minutes for people to join. Thanks for being here. Hi guys.
good_example: Share your screen with the nine-dot puzzle and challenge the audience to connect all nine dots with four straight lines without lifting the pen.
why_it_works: An experience makes the audience feel the message rather than just hear it, so they remember it far longer.
when_to_use: Especially effective in virtual presentations when people are still joining and distracted.
for_written_prose: partly — a described puzzle or visual can work in text, but live interaction and screen-sharing do not carry to the page.
source_title: How to Start a Presentation So NOBODY Checks Their Phone!

name: Look at the sentence before it
what_it_does: Ensures sentence variety by deciding whether to echo or contrast with the previous sentence.
bad_example: This sentence has five words. Here are five more words. Five word sentences are fine, but several together become monotonous.
good_example: After a series of short sentences, write a long, flowing sentence to break the rhythm.
why_it_works: Sentences are like music; knowing the previous note helps you choose the next for variety and flow.
when_to_use: When writing any sentence, especially in a sequence where rhythm matters.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Vary sentence length
what_it_does: Alternates short, medium, and long sentences to avoid monotony.
bad_example: Five word sentences in a row create a monotonous, ratatat rhythm.
good_example: Alternate short with medium with long sentences.
why_it_works: Variety in length creates musical flow and keeps the reader engaged.
when_to_use: Whenever multiple sentences appear together.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Vary sentence structure
what_it_does: Starts sentences in different ways, avoiding repetitive subject-verb-object patterns.
bad_example: He did this. He did that. He did another thing.
good_example: Today, despite Rita's closed face and pressed lips, I would like to stay here in the kitchen.
why_it_works: Different openings and structures create variety and prevent predictability.
when_to_use: When sentences feel repetitive in structure.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Vary rhythm
what_it_does: Uses rhythmic patterns like three-part lists sparingly to create flow.
bad_example: Repeating the same three-part rhythm in consecutive sentences.
good_example: We'd stare at the sun, grip the grass, hold on to each other in the dark.
why_it_works: A unique rhythm stands out and flows off the tongue, but overuse dulls it.
when_to_use: When a sentence needs a musical, flowing quality.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Cherry-pick the verb
what_it_does: Deliberately selects strong, precise verbs instead of default or plain ones.
bad_example: Heavy sunflowers bending over fences.
good_example: Heavy sunflowers weeping over fences.
why_it_works: Verbs control the sentence; a precise verb adds connotation and does more work.
when_to_use: Whenever writing a sentence, especially action or description.
when_it_backfires: Don't use fancy or obscure words; use normal words in unusual contexts.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Pick a power word
what_it_does: Includes one word per sentence that elevates it from mere information to something surprising.
bad_example: She had a rich, loud laugh.
good_example: She had a rich, naked laugh.
why_it_works: A surprising but simple word creates a vivid image and adds depth.
when_to_use: In most sentences, but not every sentence needs one.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Create a story arc
what_it_does: Structures a sentence as a mini-story that moves from one state to a different one.
bad_example: He was a handsome man with a tanned face and white hair. He had cancer.
good_example: He was still a handsome man with a tanned, chiseled face and long, thick, wavy white hair. But his cells had begun to reproduce in a haphazard fashion, destroying the DNA of neighboring cells and secreting toxins into his body.
why_it_works: The beginning sets expectations that the end inverts or fulfills, creating a journey for the reader.
when_to_use: When a sentence needs to be particularly captivating or pull its weight.
when_it_backfires: Not every sentence needs this; don't force it.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Choose a figure of speech
what_it_does: Uses rhetorical devices like metonymy, synecdoche, anaphora, epistrophe, antithesis, hyperbole, litotes, or repetition to enhance sentences.
bad_example: He threatened with his sword.
good_example: He shall think differently, the Musketeer threatened when he feels the point of my steel.
why_it_works: Figures of speech add surprise, rhythm, and depth, making sentences more memorable.
when_to_use: In many beautiful sentences, but not every sentence needs one.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Cut the fat
what_it_does: Removes unnecessary adjectives, adverbs, prepositional phrases, and redundant words to highlight nouns and verbs.
bad_example: They collaborated together on the project.
good_example: They collaborated on the project.
why_it_works: Trimming clutter makes the remaining words more powerful and direct.
when_to_use: During revision of any sentence.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Use short sentences
what_it_does: Embraces very short sentences, even three-word ones, for impact.
bad_example: Avoiding short sentences entirely.
good_example: Include at least one three-word sentence in your book.
why_it_works: Short sentences can be powerful and provide variety.
when_to_use: When a sentence needs emphasis or a break in rhythm.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I Tried a 6-Step Formula for Writing Better Sentences

name: Draw from personal experience
what_it_does: Starts a story from something that actually happened to you, then heightens it for fiction.
bad_example: I wrote exactly what happened when I was sick last year.
good_example: I had an illness in real life, but in the story I made it life-threatening.
why_it_works: Personal material carries built-in emotional weight and significance, giving the story a deeper foundation.
when_to_use: When you need a story idea with authentic emotional stakes.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video only warns not to feel constrained by literal facts.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Rotate point of view
what_it_does: Rewrites the same story from different characters' perspectives to find the best teller.
bad_example: I told it from my own point of view because that's how it happened.
good_example: I tried the neighbor's, the spouse's, the child's, even the gun's point of view.
why_it_works: Seeing the story through multiple eyes reveals which perspective has the most at stake and creates the strongest tension.
when_to_use: After you have a first draft or story idea, before committing to a narrator.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video cautions against using tricky inanimate POVs too often.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Create a ticking clock
what_it_does: Adds a countdown to a specific event that pressurizes the narrative.
bad_example: The story meandered with no clear deadline.
good_example: The chess tournament is announced at the start, and we count down to it.
why_it_works: A deadline creates suspense and gives readers a climactic event to anticipate.
when_to_use: When your story needs forward momentum and tension.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Choose a charged object
what_it_does: Selects a prop with sentimental, plot, and symbolic weight that recurs throughout the story.
bad_example: An engagement ring appeared once and was never mentioned again.
good_example: Her father's championship football ring symbolized the mindset of a champion.
why_it_works: Objects in fiction are totems with outsized power; a recurring object ties scenes together and carries meaning.
when_to_use: When you want a concrete symbol that can unify the story.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video advises avoiding cliché objects and ensuring the object is necessary.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Find the transitional moment
what_it_does: Identifies the crux when a character moves from one mode of existence to the next.
bad_example: The character stayed in the same situation throughout.
good_example: She decided to enter the chess tournament for the first time, stepping out of her comfort zone.
why_it_works: A transition creates a before-and-after that gives the story a subtle arc, even if the change is small.
when_to_use: When your story needs a turning point, especially a delicate or internal one.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video notes short story transitions can be very small, unlike movie-sized shifts.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Anchor with a world event
what_it_does: Connects the story to a real-world event, figure, or familiar situation readers recognize.
bad_example: The story floated in a void with no reference points.
good_example: Cheating at the chess tournament tapped into recent real-world chess cheating scandals.
why_it_works: Familiar references give readers an immediate emotional entry point and make the story feel true.
when_to_use: When you want to ground readers quickly and add verisimilitude.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video warns against merely name-dropping a famous person.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Set up binary forces
what_it_does: Creates opposition by making characters or forces direct opposites.
bad_example: The characters were similar and agreed with each other.
good_example: An educated one-legged PhD is duped by an uneducated Bible salesman.
why_it_works: Opposites butt heads, and the wider the gap between them, the more room for sharp conflict.
when_to_use: When your story needs tension between characters.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Shape with a plot structure
what_it_does: Applies a narrative arc such as Freytag's Pyramid or the seven-point plot structure to organize the whole story.
bad_example: The story had no rising action or climax.
good_example: The chess story followed rising action to a climax when the cheater was exposed.
why_it_works: A recognizable structure escalates events and releases emotion effectively.
when_to_use: When you need to shape the overall sequence of events.
when_it_backfires: Not stated; the video notes many famous short stories don't follow neat structures.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)

name: Experiment with form
what_it_does: Tries something formally or technically unconventional, breaking from the previous steps.
bad_example: I followed all the rules exactly and played it safe.
good_example: I wrote the story as a recipe, or made the narrator wildly unreliable.
why_it_works: Experimentation opens up new possibilities and can make a story memorable.
when_to_use: After you have a solid draft or plan, to push the story further.
for_written_prose: yes
source_title: I tried Nelson's 9 Steps for Story Writing (and it's brilliant)
